source.title: Revisiting Sample Selection Approach to Positive-Unlabeled Learning: Turning Unlabeled Data into Positive rather than Negative
source.authors: Miao Xu; B. Li; Gang Niu; Bo Han; Masashi Sugiyama

record.file_problem: not stated; the supplied text appears complete.
record.tranche_reason: The authors reimplement part of a noisy-label memorization result and report accuracy over training on clean and corrupted labels, bearing on V6.
record.gate_note: The paper's other memorization discussion and histogram figures are framed as motivation for its PU-learning method; cited prior-work findings are not recorded as this study's results. Figure 2 is the reported reimplementation relevant to V6.
record.test_reason: Figure 2 reports the authors' own reimplementation of part of Arpit et al.'s Figure 7, using training and validation accuracy over epochs under random label corruption. This directly bears on V6 through the original experimental approach and measure.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the Figure 2 interpretation: frequent patterns are learned initially, followed by noise fitting in corrupted-label conditions. The paper's main conclusion is that aaPU's selection and use of positive examples improves on nnPU on synthetic and real datasets.
record.recipe_differences: The authors say they reimplemented part of the result in Figure 7 of Arpit et al. (2017); the supplied text does not specify all implementation details.
record.problems: The reimplementation is only described as part of the prior result; model, dataset, numerical accuracies, and implementation details are not stated. Accuracy values are presented in a figure, with variance shown but not quantified in the text.
record.rows_left_out: None of the other memorization-related figures is extracted as a claim-version result: Figures 3–5 show PU loss histograms used to motivate sample selection, and Figure 6 concerns synthetic PU data selection. Cited findings from other work are excluded.

untested.parts: Complete random labeling, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Training-time ratios and convergence slowing as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily worsening test error across corruption levels extending to complete corruption.
Effects of adding or removing explicit regularization on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Learning dynamics under completely random labeling; direct measurement of separate real-label and corrupted-label learning trajectories.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source of V6. Figure 2's model, dataset, and detailed training configuration are unspecified; nearby CIFAR-10 PU configurations cannot safely be assigned to it. Support is qualitative and rests on the authors' explicit interpretation of validation dynamics. Figures 3–6 are already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: Whether standard networks fit completely random labels to zero or near-zero training error with test error at chance, without changing architecture or hyperparameters.
Training-time cost and convergence time as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Whether training error remains perfect and test error rises steadily across corruption levels while retaining signal.
Whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation prevent random-label fitting, or whether their removal harms true-label generalization.
The supplied account does not identify the model or dataset for this reimplementation, nor does it directly compare learning real labels with learning completely random labels.

rows.note: The paper describes this as fitting frequent patterns; the specific model, dataset, and accuracy values are not stated in the supplied text.
rows.check: Valid clean-label control, but its early validation-accuracy increase alone cannot establish that real patterns precede noise memorization. Retain it as context for R2–R3.

relationships.condition: Figure 2 reimplementation with 20% and 40% random label noise
relationships.reason: R2–R3 show early validation improvement followed by a drop, which Section 3.2 explicitly interprets as learning frequent patterns before fitting noise; R1 supplies the clean-label control.
relationships.display_finding: Validation accuracy improved early and then dropped at 20% and 40% noise, which the authors attributed to learning frequent patterns before noise.
